newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan executives like yen level now - BOJ official.
newsitem.headline: Japan executives like yen level now - BOJ official.

text.p: Many Japanese business executives say they want the yen's exchange rate to stabilise at around current levels, Masayuki Matsushima, director of the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) research and statistics department, told a symposium on the economy on Wednesday.

Matsushima said: "Regarding present currency levels, there aren't any big complaints among businesspeople. Many businesspeople say they want the exchange rate to stay at around current levels." The dollar was at 111.72/82 yen in late Tokyo trade on Wednesday.
The Japanese economy is gradually recovering, and it is not proper to say that it has started slowing down, he said.
"We should not be optimistic about the outlook for the economy, but we must not be overly pessimistic."
He said the speed of the economy's recovery was not accelerating.

Some people had the impression that the economy was stalled because of production adjustment in the semiconductor industry and because private consumption was hurt by such factors as slow growth in summer bonus payments and a food poisoning epidemic this summer.
"If the economy marked time, basically it was a temporary phenomenon."
He said economic growth was unlikely to be undermined by a planned increase in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent next April.
Matsushima said it was obvious Japan should solve the problem of its huge budget deficit.
The economy would not be hurt by this factor if steps that could be taken to solve the problem were made clear, he said.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) said in a statement on September 24 that the Japanese government's outstanding debt, including that in the form of government bonds, totalled 334.1 trillion yen at the end of June.
Of the total, the outstanding amount of ordinary government bonds totalled 229.8 trillion yen at the end of June, it said.
Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said on September 3 that his ministry was working towards issuing fewer deficit-financing bonds for the fiscal year starting next April than in 1996/97.

On deficit-financing bonds, Kubo admitted that it would be impossible to abolish such issues next fiscal year after looking at the 1997/98 budget requests submitted by various ministries at the end of August.
Unless budget reforms were carried out, it was "highly possible" that MOF might be forced to issue more than 12 trillion yen worth of deficit-financing bonds this fiscal year, Kubo said.
